tiles.alt: CHAPTER SIX / The Planning Fallacy
Some children would have waited until after their first trip to Diagon Alley. Most would at least have waited to get their wands first. / Harry: Bag of element 79.
Harry's pencil lab notes on the pouch: some phrasings retrieve the gold, some don't. / Harry James Potter-Evans-Verres had got his hands on at least one magical item. Why wait?

Harry: Professor, can you give me two words—one for gold, and one for something else that isn't money—in a language I wouldn't know? Don't tell me which is which. / McGonagall: Ahava and zahav. That's Hebrew. The other one means love.
More notes: "ahava" fails, "zahav" works; "115 Galleons" works but "90 plus 25 Galleons" doesn't.

Harry: AAAAAARGH THIS DOESN'T MAKE ANY SENSE! / Harry: It can count but it can't add? It understands nouns but not noun phrases that mean the same thing? It's not using the maker's knowledge and it's not using mine—
McGonagall: Magic.
Harry: That's just a word! Even after you say it, I can't make any new predictions! It's exactly like saying "phlogiston"!
McGonagall: With respect, Mr Potter, I'm quite sure I don't understand what you're trying to do. Unless—this is just a guess, mind—you're trying to take over the world?
Harry: No! I mean yes—well, no! / McGonagall: I think I should perhaps be alarmed that you have trouble answering the question.
Harry: How many Muggle-raised children do you get at Hogwarts every year? / McGonagall: Perhaps ten or so?
Harry: TEN?
Harry's notes: either magic is so impenetrable that everyone gave up — or the whole world is his for the taking. A little flag planted on a globe.

Harry thrusts a fist at the sky in the middle of Diagon Alley. / You're mine now, Harry thought at the walls of Diagon Alley—at all the lands and people of wizarding Britain, and the entire universe of which Muggle scientists understood so much less than they believed. / I, Harry James Potter-Evans-Verres, do now claim this territory in the name of Science.
A perfectly calm, cloudless sky. / Lightning and thunder completely failed to flash and boom in the cloudless skies.
McGonagall: What are you smiling about? / Harry: I'm wondering if there's a spell to make lightning flash in the background whenever I make an ominous resolution.
McGonagall: I have the distinct feeling that I ought to be doing something about this.
Harry had bought his potion ingredients and cauldron, and, oh, a few more things. Smart, sensible purchases. He genuinely didn't understand why Professor McGonagall was looking so suspicious.

The Emergency Healing Pack Plus, open: self-tightening tourniquets, a syringe of liquid fire, numbing cloth, a "Dementor Exposure Treatment" that looks exactly like chocolate, and a Bafflesnaffle Counter shaped like a quivering egg. / The Emergency Healing Pack Plus.
Harry: A definite buy at five Galleons, wouldn't you agree?
What he was getting instead could only be described as the Evil Eye.
McGonagall: And just why do you expect to need a healer's kit, young man?

Harry: You think I'm planning to do something dangerous, and that's why I want a medical kit? / Harry: Were you also thinking that when I bought the Feather-Fall Potion, the Gillyweed, and the Food and Water Pills?
McGonagall: Yes. / Harry: Just what sort of plan do you think I have going, here?
McGonagall: I don't know. But it ends either in you delivering a ton of silver to Gringotts, or in world domination.
Harry: World domination is such an ugly phrase. I prefer to call it world optimisation.
This hilarious joke failed to reassure the witch giving him the Look of Doom.
Harry: Don't take this the wrong way, Professor McGonagall, but what sort of crazy children are you used to dealing with?
McGonagall: Gryffindors. / The word carried a freight of bitterness and despair that fell like an eternal curse on all youthful enthusiasm and high spirits.

Harry: I am not going to be in Gryffindor. I am going to be in Ravenclaw. I don't like danger, it is scary. I am being prudent. I am preparing for unforeseen contingencies! / Harry: Like my parents used to sing: Be prepared! That's the Boy Scout's marching song!
McGonagall: And what sort of contingency do you imagine this kit might prepare you for, young man?

Imagined, in cold blues: a girl in school robes lying on stone; Harry on his knees beside her, digging desperately in his pouch. / "One of my classmates gets bitten by a horrible monster. And as I scrabble frantically in my pouch for something that could help her, she looks at me sadly, and with her last breath says—" / "Why weren't you prepared?"
"And then she dies, and I know as her eyes close that she won't ever forgive me—"
The young salesgirl stares at Harry, lips pressed tight. / Della: (a small gasp)
Then she whirled, and fled into the back of the shop.
Harry: What…?

McGonagall leads Harry into an alley that dead-ends in black earth, and seals off the sound with her wand. / McGonagall: Quietus. / A screen of silence descended around them, blocking out all the street noises.
McGonagall: You must remember, Mr Potter, that there was a war in this country not ten years ago. / McGonagall: Everyone has lost someone. To speak of friends dying in your arms is not done lightly.
Harry: The war ended ten years ago. So that girl would have been eight, maybe nine, when—when—
Harry: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry! / He turned to run from the older witch's gaze—but there was a wall of dirt blocking his way, and he didn't have his wand yet.
McGonagall: I know you are, Mr Potter.
Harry: Did anything like that happen to— / And then Harry shut his lips, and slapped a hand over his mouth for good measure.
McGonagall: You must learn to think before you speak, Mr Potter, or go through life without many friends. That has been the fate of many a Ravenclaw. I hope it will not be yours.

McGonagall: But to answer your question: no. Certainly I've watched a friend breathe their last, once or seven times. / McGonagall: But not one of them ever cursed me as they died. Why would you say such a thing, Mr Potter? Why would you even think it?
Harry: I—I—it's just that I always try to imagine the worst thing that could happen. / McGonagall: But why? / Harry: So I can stop it from happening!

McGonagall: Mr Potter. It's not your responsibility to take care of the students at Hogwarts. It's mine. I won't let anything bad happen to you or anyone else. / McGonagall: You won't need a healer's kit at all, let alone a five-Galleon one.
Harry: But I do! Nowhere is perfectly safe! What if my parents have a heart attack when I go home for Christmas—Madam Pomfrey won't be there—
McGonagall: There's no need to think about such terrible things, Mr Potter!
Harry: Yes there is! If you don't think, you don't just get hurt yourself—you end up hurting other people!
Professor McGonagall opened her mouth, then closed it. / McGonagall: Mr Potter… if I were to offer to listen to you, for a while… is there anything you'd like to talk to me about?
Harry: About what?
McGonagall: About why you're convinced you must always be on your guard against terrible things happening to you.

A pencil bar chart: of students 50%, 75% and 99% sure they'd finish their homework in time, only 13%, 19% and 45% did. / Harry: Muggle researchers found people are always too optimistic. Even when they were 99% sure, less than half the students finished on time. It's called the planning fallacy.

Harry: So when you're doing something new, you have to be really, really pessimistic. So pessimistic that reality comes out better as often as it comes out worse. / Harry: Like, I make this big effort to be gloomy and imagine one classmate getting bitten—but what actually happens is that the surviving Death Eaters attack the whole school to get at me. But on a happier note—
McGonagall: Stop.
McGonagall: I think I might not have made myself clear. Did anything happen to you personally that frightened you, Mr Potter?
Harry: What happened to me personally is only anecdotal evidence. It doesn't carry the same weight as a replicated, peer-reviewed study with random assignment.
McGonagall: I would still like to hear about it.

Memory, sepia: Mum, laughing, hands a much younger Harry a saucepan. He is pleading. / "There'd been some muggings in our neighbourhood. Mum asked me to return a pan to a neighbour two streets away. I said I didn't want to, because I might get mugged." / Mum: Harry, don't say things like that!

Memory: tiny Harry walks alone down a dim street, clutching a saucepan, terrified. / "Like thinking about it would make it happen. So if I didn't talk about it, I'd be safe." / "I was too young to know how unlikely it was. But I was old enough to know that not thinking about something doesn't stop it from happening. So I was really scared."

Harry: She wouldn't listen. I begged her not to send me out, and she laughed it off. / Harry: That's when I realised that everyone who was supposed to protect me was actually crazy. And that I couldn't ever rely on them to get anything right.
There was a long silence. / Harry didn't like himself when he was angry.
McGonagall: Thank you for sharing that, Mr Potter. I shall have to think about this. / (Almost exactly the look Harry wore while experimenting on the pouch—if he'd only had a mirror to see it.)
Harry: Um. Can we go get the healer's kit now? / McGonagall: And if I say no—that it is too expensive and you won't need it—then what?
Harry: Exactly what you're thinking, Professor. I conclude you're another crazy adult I can't talk to—and I start planning how to get my hands on a healer's kit anyway.
McGonagall: I am your guardian on this trip. I will not allow you to push me around.
Harry: I understand. / Professor McGonagall had told him to think before he spoke. He probably wouldn't remember that tomorrow, but he could at least remember it for five minutes.
The witch's wand made a slight circle, and the noises of Diagon Alley came back. / McGonagall: All right, young man. Let's go get that healer's kit.
Harry's jaw drops.
Della: I'm sorry— / Harry: I apologise for— / Della: I didn't mean to get you in trouble with Professor McGonagall. I hope she wasn't too awful to you.
McGonagall: Della!
Harry: Don't worry. I understand that she's only awful to me because she loves me. / Harry: One Emergency Healing Pack Plus, please.
The pouch's Widening Lip swallows the briefcase-sized kit. It burps. / glurp / burp / Harry swore he heard a small burping sound afterwards. That had to have been spelled in on purpose.
McGonagall: Small pets are permitted at Hogwarts. You could get an owl to send letters, for example— / Harry: Can I pay a Knut or something and rent an owl when I need one?
McGonagall: Yes. / Harry: Then I think emphatically no.
Harry: I had a pet rock once. It died.

Harry: I could take care of it. But I'd end up obsessing all day about whether I'd remembered to feed it, or if it was slowly starving in its cage, wondering where its master was. / McGonagall: That poor owl. Abandoned like that. I wonder what it would do.
Harry: Well, I expect it'd get really hungry and start trying to claw its way out of the cage, though it probably wouldn't have much luck with—
Harry stops short.
Harry: That owl does not represent me! My parents never locked me in a cupboard and left me to starve! I do not have abandonment issues, and I don't like the trend of your thoughts!
Harry: You think I was… I was abused? / McGonagall: Were you?

Harry, screaming, in a red blaze of fury. / Harry: NO! I know about child abuse, and if anything like that happened I would call the police! But my parents never did anything like that, never ever! / Harry: An accusation like that can destroy families even when the parents are completely innocent! Don't you dare threaten my family with that! I won't let you destroy my home!
McGonagall: Harry— / Harry took a fast step back, and his hand snapped up and knocked hers away.

McGonagall: Harry, it's all right. I believe you. / McGonagall: I saw your house. I saw you with your parents. They love you. You love them. But I had to ask, because there is something strange at work here.

McGonagall: When you're happy, you don't behave like an abused child. Not at all. You smile at strangers. I put my hand on your shoulder and you didn't flinch. / McGonagall: But sometimes—only sometimes—you say or do something that seems very much like someone who spent his first eleven years locked in a cellar.
Harry: And how do you explain your observations, Professor McGonagall?
McGonagall: I don't know. But it's possible that something could have happened to you that you don't remember.
Harry: Suppressed memory is a load of pseudo-science! People don't repress traumatic memories, they remember them all too well!
McGonagall: No, Mr Potter. There is a Charm called Obliviation.
Harry: A spell that erases memories? / McGonagall: But not all the effects of the experience, if you see what I'm saying.

Harry: Professor—how sure are you of your observations? And what alternative explanations could there be? / McGonagall: Sure? I'm sure of nothing. In all my life I've never met anyone like you. Sometimes you just don't seem eleven years old—or even all that human.
McGonagall: I'm sorry! That came out sounding different from what I had in mind—
Harry: On the contrary, Professor McGonagall. I shall take it as a very great compliment. / Harry: But may I offer an alternative explanation?

Harry: Children aren't meant to be too much smarter than their parents. Or too much saner. I'm too smart, Professor. I've got nothing to say to normal children. Adults don't respect me enough to really talk to me. / Harry: I'm isolated. I've been isolated my whole life. Maybe that has some of the same effects as being locked in a cellar. / Harry: And I also have an anger management problem. But I'm working on it. That's all.
McGonagall: That's all?
Harry: That's all. Surely, Professor, even in magical Britain, the normal explanation is always worth considering?
The two of them stand in the dead-end alley, quiet, in lengthening shadows. / Professor McGonagall didn't say whether she agreed.
To be continued
